children: In the paragraph below even at the peak of Stephen’s rigorous religious discipline, he still has doubts that he has done enough. This is typical and unsurprising, after all, even if God himself showed up and were to tell him that all what he has done is enough, he would probably still have doubts. This is shown below, “A restless feeling of guilt would always be present with him: he would confess and repent and be absolved, confess and repent again and be absolved again, fruitlessly. Perhaps that first hasty confession wrung from him by the fear of hell had not been good? Perhaps, concerned only for his imminent doom, he had not had sincere sorrow for his sin?” This is the old Stephen we know and love, not the passive, unquestioning person we’ve seen most of the time in this chapter. His nagging dissatisfaction is what lets us know that Stephen’s destiny does not lie in the religious life.
